stories.title_en: Posing as Daoists to Swindle the Salt Censor

paragraphs.zh: 唐寅，字伯虎，又字子畏，南京吴趋里人也。中弘治戊午南京解元，因事被黜之。后遂放浪不羁，流留花酒。善诗文，画极工。与文征明、文征仲、祝希哲等为友，皆极一时之名流也。日游平康妓家，滑稽为乐，随口成文。有一皂隶，携纸一张求画。伯虎援笔，画螺蛳十餘个，题诗于上云：“不是蝤蛑不是蛏，海味之中少此名。千呼万呼呼不出，只待人来打窟臀。”众皆大笑。偶一日出，见县前枷一和尚。众人请曰：“可将此和尚作诗一首。”伯虎询知和尚被枷缘由，援笔题于枷上曰：“皂隶官差去采茶，不要纹银只要赊。县里捉来三十板，方盘托出大西瓜。”知县送客出来见之，问是何人所作，或以伯虎对，即将和尚释之。其捷于口才，大约类此。
paragraphs.en: Tang Yin, courtesy name Bohu, also Ziwei, was from Wuqu Lane in Nanjing. He placed first in the Hongzhi wuwu (1498) Nanjing provincial examination, then lost his degree over a scandal. After that he lived without restraint, lingering among flowers and wine. He was skilled at poetry and prose, and especially at painting. He was friends with Wen Zhengming, Wen Zhengzhong, Zhu Xizhe, and others—all famous men of that generation. Day after day he visited the pleasure houses, making jokes for fun and composing as soon as his mouth opened. A yamen runner once brought a sheet of paper and asked for a painting. Bohu took up the brush, painted a dozen or so snails, and wrote on it: “Not a swimming crab, not a razor clam; among seafood this one barely has a name. Call a thousand times, ten thousand times, it will not come out; it only waits for someone to smack its hole-rump.” Everyone laughed hard. One day he went out and saw a monk in a cangue in front of the county yamen. People asked him to make a poem on the monk. Bohu asked why the monk had been cangued, then wrote on the cangue: “The runner, sent on official business, went to pick tea; he wanted no fine silver, only goods on credit. The county seized him for thirty strokes; on a square tray they served up a big watermelon.” The magistrate, seeing guests out, noticed it, asked who had written it, was told it was Bohu, and promptly released the monk. His ready tongue was generally of this kind.

paragraphs.zh: 一日，与祝希哲等十数辈，携装游维扬，日与妓者饮酒，声色为乐。将及一月，资用殆尽。希哲曰：“黄金用尽，作何计策乎？”伯虎曰：“无妨！当今盐使者，资财巨万。我和你二人，可假扮女贞观道士以化之。”二人即扮道士。值盐使者升堂，二人俯伏阶下，云：“女贞观道士参见。”盐使者大怒曰：“岂不闻御史台风霜凛凛耶？是何道者，敢此无状！”将挞之。二人徐对曰：“明公以小道为游方觅食者耶？小道遍游天下，所交者皆极海内名流。即如吴邑唐伯虎、文征明、祝希哲辈，无不与小道折节为友。凡诗词歌赋，应口辄成。明公如不信，愿奏薄技，惟明公所命。”盐使者乃指堂下石牛为题，命二人联诗一首。伯虎应声即吟云：“嵯峨怪石倚云边，”哲云：“抛掷于今定几年。”虎云：“台藓作毛因雨长，”哲云：“藤萝穿鼻任风牵。”虎云：“从来不食溪边草，”哲云：“自古难耕陇上田。”虎云：“怪杀牧童鞭不起，”哲云：“笛声斜挂夕阳烟。”
paragraphs.en: One day, with Zhu Xizhe and a dozen others, he packed up and traveled to Weiyang. Day after day they drank with courtesans and made music and beauty their pleasure. After nearly a month their money was almost gone. Xizhe said, “The gold is spent—what’s the plan?” Bohu said, “No matter. The Salt Censor these days is worth tens of thousands. You and I can pose as Daoist priests of Nüzhen Abbey and tap him for it.” The two dressed as Daoists. When the Salt Censor held court they knelt at the foot of the steps and said, “Daoist priests of Nüzhen Abbey present themselves.” The Salt Censor was furious: “Have you not heard that an inspector’s court is frost and wind? What kind of Daoists dare this insolence!” He was about to have them beaten. The two answered calmly: “Does Your Honor take us for wandering priests begging meals? We have traveled the whole empire; those we keep company with are all famous men within the seas. Even Tang Bohu, Wen Zhengming, and Zhu Xizhe of Wu county treat us as friends without standing on rank. Poetry, lyrics, songs, rhapsodies—we finish them as soon as the mouth opens. If Your Honor does not believe us, we offer a small sample; command us as you please.” The Salt Censor pointed to a stone ox below the hall and ordered them to compose a linked verse. Bohu answered at once: “A towering strange rock leans against the clouds.” Zhe: “Thrown down—who can tell how many years by now.” Hu: “Moss on the terrace makes its hair, grown by the rain.” Zhe: “Vines thread its nose, left for the wind to tug.” Hu: “It has never eaten grass beside the stream.” Zhe: “From of old it could never plow the ridge fields.” Hu: “No wonder the herdboy’s whip cannot raise it.” Zhe: “His flute hangs aslant in the sunset haze.”

paragraphs.zh: 盐使者览毕，霁色问曰：“诗则佳矣。将欲何为？”二人曰：“顷者女贞观圮坏。闻明公宽仁好施，愿捐俸金修葺，以成胜事，亦且不朽。”盐使者大悦，即檄吴兴二县，可给库银五百与之。二人见盐使者应允，速夜赴吴兴，假为道士说关节行状，对吴兴二县云：“今有盐使者修葺女贞观，此系盛举，可依数与之，不可宽缓。”吴兴二县果如数与之。二人得银大悦，曰：“不将万丈深潭计，安得骊龙项下珠？”复往维扬，聚交游十数辈，于妓者家欢呼剧饮，纵其所乐。不十数日，五百之金费用殆尽。后盐使者按临吴兴，束衣冠往女贞观，则见其倾圯如故。召吴兴二县责之，二县对曰：“日前唐伯虎与祝希哲从维扬来，极称明公兴此盛举，小知县即依数与之矣。”盐使者怅然，知为二人所骗，但惜其才，故亦不究。
paragraphs.en: The Salt Censor finished reading, his face softened, and he asked, “The poem is fine. What do you want?” The two said, “Nüzhen Abbey has lately fallen into ruin. We hear Your Honor is generous and fond of giving. If you would donate salary to repair it, it would complete a worthy deed, and the merit would not fade.” The Salt Censor was delighted and issued a directive to the two counties of Wuxing: issue five hundred taels from the treasury to them. Seeing that he had agreed, the two hurried that very night to Wuxing, posed as Daoists carrying the Censor’s instructions, and told the two counties: “The Salt Censor is repairing Nüzhen Abbey. This is a grand undertaking. Give the sum as ordered; do not delay.” The two counties paid it in full. The two men, delighted with the silver, said, “If we had not reckoned on the ten-thousand-fathom pool, how would we have got the pearl under the black dragon’s chin?” They went back to Weiyang, gathered their dozen companions, shouted and drank in the courtesans’ houses, and did as they pleased. In fewer than ten days the five hundred taels were gone. Later the Salt Censor toured Wuxing, put on his robes and cap, and went to Nüzhen Abbey—only to find it still in ruins as before. He summoned the two counties and rebuked them. They answered, “The other day Tang Bohu and Zhu Xizhe came from Weiyang and praised Your Honor for raising this grand work; we magistrates paid the sum as ordered.” The Salt Censor was dismayed, knew he had been taken in by the two men, but valued their talent, so he did not pursue it.

paragraphs.zh: 按：唐伯虎、祝希哲，皆海内一时名家也。但以不得志于时，遂纵于声色，青楼酒肆中，无不闻其名。然非口若悬河，才高倚马，何以能倾动使院？此之骗，可谓骗之善矣。独计当今冠进贤而坐虎皮者，咸思削民脂以润私橐，敛众怨以肥身家，其所以骗民者何如！乃一旦反为唐、祝所骗，亦可为贪墨者一儆。但其知而不究，亦可谓有怜才之心者矣。
paragraphs.en: Note: Tang Bohu and Zhu Xizhe were both famous men of their generation within the seas. Blocked in their careers, they gave themselves to music and beauty; there was no brothel or wineshop that had not heard their names. Yet without tongues like rivers in flood and talent that could draft as fast as a horse can run, how could they have shaken the Censor’s yamen? This swindle may be called a swindle well done. Consider today’s men in the “worthy-and-good” cap, sitting on tiger skins: they all think of scraping the people’s fat to grease their private bags, gathering the crowd’s resentment to fatten their households—and how they swindle the people! Then one day they themselves are swindled by Tang and Zhu, which may serve as a warning to the greedy. That the Censor knew and still did not prosecute may also be called a heart that pities talent.

stories.title_en: Chen Quan’s Scheme to Sleep with a Famous Courtesan

paragraphs.zh: 金陵陈全者，百万巨富也。其为人风流潇洒，尤善滑稽。凡见一物，能速成口号。尝与本地院妓往来，唯一妓最得意。夏间瓜初出，院妓将瓜皮二片，放于门限内，诈令一人慌忙叫全云：“某姐姐偶得危病，要你一相见方瞑目。”全即乘马速至，慌忙进门，脚踹瓜皮跌倒。众妓鼓掌大笑云：“陈官人快做一口号，不得迟！”全即答曰：“陈全走得忙，院子安排定。只因两块皮，几丧我的命。”众妓欣然，遂会饮而罢。
paragraphs.en: Chen Quan of Jinling was a man of enormous wealth. He was easy in manner and especially good at jokes. Whatever he saw, he could turn into a doggerel verse at once. He used to go back and forth with the local registered courtesans; one of them was his particular favorite. In summer, when the first melons came out, the house put two pieces of melon rind just inside the threshold and sent someone running to shout to Quan: “Sister So-and-so has suddenly taken a mortal illness; she wants to see you once before she closes her eyes.” Quan mounted at once and rode hard. He rushed in, stepped on the rind, and fell. The courtesans clapped and laughed: “Master Chen, make a verse at once—no delay!” Quan answered: “Chen Quan came in a rush; the house had it all arranged. Just because of two pieces of rind, I nearly lost my life.” The women were pleased, and they drank together and left it at that.

paragraphs.zh: 又一日，与众妓游湖，见新造一船。众妓云：“速作一口号，勿迟！”全即答曰：“新造船儿一只，当初拟采红莲。于今反作渡头船，来往千千万万。有钱接他上渡，无钱丢在一边。上湿下漏未曾干，隔岸郎君又唤。”众妓皆欢然叹服。凡游戏口号，类如此。
paragraphs.en: Another day he was out on the lake with several courtesans and saw a newly built boat. They said, “Make a verse at once—don’t lag!” Quan answered: “A brand-new little boat; it was meant at first to pick red lotuses. Now it is a ferry at the crossing, coming and going by the thousands. Those with money are taken aboard; those without are tossed aside. Wet above, leaking below, never dry—and from the far bank another gentleman is calling.” The courtesans all laughed and admired him. His joking verses were generally of this kind.

paragraphs.zh: 彼时，浙江杭州有一名妓，号花不如。姿态甚佳，且琴棋诗画，无不通晓。但身价颇高，不与庸俗往来，唯与豪俊交接。每宿一夜，费银六七两方得。全闻之，欲嫖此妓，因而骗之。故令十餘家丁，陆续运船到杭，彼与二三家丁先往。到花不如家，即令家人扛抬皮箱一个———下面俱系纸包砖石，上面一重，俱是纸包真银，每十两为一封———入花不如卧房内，当面开箱取银，赏赐妓家诸役甚厚，奉不如白金十两。不如与众役俱大欢喜，以为此大财主也，所得必不资矣。不如问曰：“客官贵处？”全曰：“金陵。”又问曰：“高姓？”答曰：“姓浪。”又问曰：“尊号？”答曰：“子遂。”不如整盛席相款。子遂不去，只在彼家。过两日，又一家人来报云：“某号船已到。”子遂云：“餘货只放船内，但扛抬皮箱进姐姐家来。”如是者三四次，皮箱有五六个在不如卧房内矣。子遂见不如带珠，云：“你这珠俱不好。我有大珠数百颗，个个俱圆，候此号船到，我去取与你。”
paragraphs.en: At that time Hangzhou in Zhejiang had a famous courtesan called Hua Buru. Her looks were excellent, and she was versed in qin, chess, poetry, and painting. But her price was high. She did not mix with ordinary men, only with the rich and distinguished. A night with her cost six or seven taels. Quan heard of her and wanted to sleep with her, so he set out to swindle her. He had a dozen or more household men send boats on to Hangzhou one after another, while he and two or three servants went first. At Hua Buru’s house he had a leather chest carried in—the bottom layers all paper packets of brick and stone; the top layer all paper packets of real silver, ten taels to a packet—into Hua Buru’s bedroom. In front of everyone he opened the chest, took out silver, tipped the house servants very generously, and presented Buru with ten taels of white silver. Buru and the servants were all delighted, thinking this was a great rich man and that what they would get would be beyond counting. Buru asked, “Where is the guest from?” Quan said, “Jinling.” “Your surname?” “Lang.” “Your courtesy name?” “Zisui.” Buru laid a rich feast. Zisui did not leave; he stayed in her house. After two days another servant came to report: “Boat number such-and-such has arrived.” Zisui said, “Leave the other goods on the boat; just carry the leather chests into Sister’s house.” This happened three or four times, until five or six chests were in Buru’s bedroom. Zisui saw Buru wearing pearls and said, “These pearls of yours are all poor. I have several hundred large pearls, every one round. When this next boat arrives I will fetch them for you.”

paragraphs.zh: 将及月餘，子遂欲心已足。有一家人来报云：“某号船到。”子遂对不如言曰：“此号船不比前船，俱是实落宝货，须我自去一看，兼取大珠与你。其皮箱数个，安顿在你卧房，你须照管，我午后方能进来。但叫你家丁一人，并头口一个，同我去。”不如遂令一人跟随，并驴仔一个，与子遂同去。
paragraphs.en: After more than a month Zisui’s desire was satisfied. A servant came to report: “Boat number such-and-such has arrived.” Zisui said to Buru, “This boat is not like the earlier ones. It is all solid treasure. I must go look myself, and fetch the large pearls for you as well. The several leather chests are in your bedroom; you must watch them. I cannot come back until afternoon. Just send one of your men and one mount with me.” Buru sent a man and a donkey to go with Zisui.

paragraphs.zh: 行至半路，子遂慌忙言曰：“我钥匙一把，安放在你姐姐房内，一时起身，未及带来，你要去取来。”其人即回取。子遂云：“且止！要有我亲手字去，你姐姐方肯把钥匙交付与你。不然，取不来。”子遂乃下驴入纸店，写一口号云：“杭州花不如，接着金台浪子遂，着了人，赔了驴。从今别后，哪得明珠？”封识与那人回。不如开封视之，知被骗矣。忙开皮箱一看，俱系砖石。子遂预令家人买舟俟候，一到河边，即上舟回京。后不如细访，亦知是南京陈全，然已无如之何矣。
paragraphs.en: Halfway there Zisui said in a hurry, “I left a key in your sister’s room. I got up in a rush and did not bring it. You must go back and fetch it.” The man turned to go. Zisui said, “Wait! You will need a note in my own hand, or your sister will not give you the key. Otherwise you will not get it.” Zisui got off the donkey, went into a paper shop, and wrote a verse: “Hangzhou’s Hua Buru took in Jintai’s Lang Zisui; she was taken in, and she paid a donkey. From this parting on, where will she get bright pearls?” He sealed it and sent the man back. Buru opened it, saw she had been swindled, and hurriedly opened the chests—all brick and stone. Zisui had already told his men to hire a boat and wait; as soon as he reached the river he boarded and went back to the capital. Later Buru inquired carefully and learned it was Chen Quan of Nanjing, but there was nothing she could do.

paragraphs.zh: 按：妓家尝是骗人，轻者丧家，重者丧身，未尝有被人骗者；况花不如高抬身价，选拣孤老，其骗人财尤难计算。岂知有陈全之术，又有神出鬼没者乎！赔人赔驴，悔无及矣。此虽陈全之不羁，亦足供笼络院之一笑云。
paragraphs.en: Note: Brothels are used to swindling people. The lighter cases ruin a household; the heavier ones cost a life. One rarely hears of them being swindled themselves. Hua Buru, moreover, put her price high and picked her patrons; the wealth she took from men is past counting. Who would have thought Chen Quan had a method still more like spirits coming and going? She lost a man and a donkey, and regret came too late. This was Chen Quan’s lack of restraint, yet it is also good for a laugh at how the pleasure houses can be played.

stories.title_en: Planting Fake Ingots to Swindle a Village Farmer

paragraphs.zh: 昔有一人，本农家者流也。辛苦耕田，服食淡薄，而性甚悭吝，家颇充裕。外地有骗棍到此地方，知这乡农性贪识惘，遂探其某日当在某处耕田，预将假元宝二个重一百两，埋藏其处。俟乡农正在力耕之时，贼棍故意在其山畔，作左寻右寻状。乡农问曰：“你这人在此寻甚么？”棍云：“我在此寻些东西，你问我则甚？”乡农只得默然。棍又认此树，复认彼树，如有所失状。乡农又曰：“你这人好笑，只管满山认树何为？”棍曰：“实不相瞒，我先父往岁曾被流贼所劫，亦同入伙。后来银子甚多，孤身难带，将银埋在各处，留下一帐登记，欲再来取，不幸死矣。今我依帐来寻此处树下的，不知哪个树是。幸遇你在此，可来助我寻。若寻得，分些与你不妨。”乡农遂带锄同寻。果在一树下，寻得元宝二个。棍佯作喜甚之态，说：“此若寻得，则他处皆可寻了。我实肯分些与你，只是此处无槌凿。”又曰：“此银我无贮藏所在，不如去你家下，代我寻完，分数个元宝谢你，尊意如何？”乡农云：“甚好。”但我与你素不相识，一旦至家下来往，岂不招人疑猜？”棍云：“当诈称是何亲故方好。”乡农云：“有了。我有一妻舅，六七岁时曾卖外江客人，至今并无下落。只认作我妻舅，回来看取姊姊、姊夫，有何不可？”遂将妻父、妻母姓名形状，一一对棍说讫。
paragraphs.en: There was once a man of the farming class. He worked the fields hard, ate and dressed poorly, and was extremely stingy, yet his household was fairly well off. Swindlers from elsewhere came to the place, learned that this farmer was greedy and slow-witted, found out on which day he would be working a certain plot, and in advance buried two fake yuanbao ingots, a hundred taels in weight, at that spot. While the farmer was putting his strength into the plow, the swindler deliberately walked the hillside, pretending to search left and right. The farmer asked, “What are you looking for here?” The swindler said, “I am looking for something. Why do you ask?” The farmer fell silent. The swindler then studied this tree, then that tree, as if he had lost something. The farmer said again, “You are a funny fellow—why keep matching trees all over the hill?” The swindler said, “I will not hide it. Years ago my late father was seized by wandering bandits and even joined their band. Later he had so much silver he could not carry it alone, so he buried it in various places and left a register. He meant to come back for it, but unfortunately he died. Now I am following the register to look under a tree here, and I do not know which tree it is. Luckily I have met you. Help me look. If we find it, I will share some with you; that is no trouble.” The farmer took a hoe and went with him. Sure enough, under one tree they found two yuanbao. The swindler put on a look of great joy and said, “If we found this, the other places can all be found. I truly am willing to share some with you, only there is no hammer and chisel here.” He added, “I have nowhere to store this silver. Better go to your house. Help me finish the search, and I will thank you with several ingots. How does that sit with you?” The farmer said, “Very good. But you and I are strangers. If you suddenly come and go at my house, will people not grow suspicious?” The swindler said, “Then what relative should we pretend I am?” The farmer said, “I have it. I had a wife’s younger brother who, at six or seven, was sold to a traveler from the outer Yangzi; to this day there has been no word of him. Just take yourself for my wife’s brother, come back to see his sister and brother-in-law. Why not?” He then told the swindler one by one the names and looks of his wife’s father and mother.

paragraphs.zh: 遂领至家下，叫妻子出来见舅。其妻相见，问：“弟弟面貌，如何与我不相类？”棍应云：“弟出外省，那边风水不同，以此不类。”其妻又问云：“我父何名，形状何如？母何名，形状何如？”其棍对言不差。又问：“我叔何名，形状何如？”棍应曰：“我小时出去，只记得父母，记不得叔了。”妻遂信之。杀鸡烹鲜，设为盛馔，以待其弟。乡农兄弟诸人，各设席相待甚厚。棍对姊夫曰：“我要些零碎银用，可在你家取过十五六两，与我杂用。”乡农遂取己真银十餘两，与棍用。
paragraphs.en: He led him home and called his wife out to meet her “younger brother.” When they met she asked, “Why does my younger brother’s face not resemble mine?” The swindler said, “I went out to another province; the local air and water are different, so I do not look like you.” She asked again, “What was my father’s name, and what did he look like? What was my mother’s name, and what did she look like?” The swindler answered without a slip. She asked, “What was my uncle’s name, and what did he look like?” He said, “I left as a child. I remember only my parents, not my uncle.” The wife believed him. She killed a chicken, cooked fresh food, and set a rich meal for her “brother.” The farmer’s brothers and the rest of the family each laid feasts and treated him very well. The swindler said to his “brother-in-law,” “I need some small silver for expenses. Let me take fifteen or sixteen taels from your house for mixed use.” The farmer then took more than ten taels of his own genuine silver and gave it to the swindler.

paragraphs.zh: 过数日，棍将帐与姊夫查，更有元宝十餘个，在某山某庵中。其庵无人居住，姊夫带饮食二盒，挑至庵中。时庵中棍已预令二贼在彼伺候，即将乡农背缚于柱中。其二贼抽出牛尾尖刀，再三要杀之。棍佯劝云：“我受姊夫厚款，吃得他兄弟鸡鱼多，勿杀我姊夫。”三贼将饮食吃了即去。其乡农叫天不应，入地无门。至次日午后，一牧童至，乡农叫救命，得解缚归家。妻子问曰：“何待今日方归？舅何不回？”乡农应曰：“勿说他，勿说他。”至今被人骗者，俗语曰“勿说他”。
paragraphs.en: After a few days the swindler checked the register with his brother-in-law: there were still a dozen or more yuanbao in a certain hermitage on a certain hill. The hermitage was uninhabited. The brother-in-law carried two boxes of food and went there. Two other thieves, whom the swindler had already stationed in the hermitage, were waiting. They tied the farmer’s arms behind him to a pillar. The two drew ox-tail daggers and again and again made as if to kill him. The swindler pretended to plead: “I have been treated richly by my brother-in-law and have eaten many of his family’s chickens and fish. Do not kill my sister’s husband.” The three thieves ate the food and left. The farmer called to heaven and got no answer, called to earth and found no door. The next day, in the afternoon, a herdboy came by. The farmer shouted for help and was untied and went home. His wife asked, “Why only come back today? Why did my brother not return?” The farmer said, “Don’t speak of him, don’t speak of him.” To this day, when people have been swindled, the saying is “don’t speak of him.”

paragraphs.zh: 近有江源地方一人，被一棍亦如此骗。其妻有智，即以其元宝凿来与他，知是锡。遂将此棍捆打，勒其供状，始释之。苟非其妻有识，亦蹈前乡农覆辙也。彼时悔之，宁不晚乎！
paragraphs.en: Recently a man in Jiangyuan was swindled in the same way. His wife had wits. She had the yuanbao chiseled and given to her, and knew it was tin. They then bound and beat the swindler, forced a written confession from him, and only then let him go. If his wife had not had sense, he too would have followed this farmer’s ruts. To regret it then—would that not have been too late?

paragraphs.zh: 按：此乡农心苦力勤，啬用薄奉以致富，幸矣！何乃为贪心所使，落贼牢笼，以致失财被辱，反不如江源之妇之智哉！然末世滋伪，奸宄百出，近有丢包贼骗人甚多。更江淮间，又有扯遂法，尤难防检。贼止问你一句，你若答应一句，即被他迷。此妖术也，害人尤多。世道人心，一变至此极乎！偶因前事，遂备述之，以为出途者警。
paragraphs.en: Note: This farmer toiled in mind and body, spent little and lived thin, and so grew rich—fortunate enough! Why let greed drive him into the thieves’ cage, so that he lost money and was humiliated, and fell short even of the Jiangyuan woman’s wits? Yet in these latter days deceit multiplies and villains come in a hundred shapes. Lately the “drop-the-bundle” thieves have taken in a great many people. And between the Yangzi and the Huai there is also the “pull-along” method, still harder to guard against. The thief asks you only one sentence; if you answer even one sentence, you are bewitched. This is demonic art, and it harms still more people. Have the world’s ways and men’s hearts changed to this extreme? I set it down because of the foregoing, as a warning to those who go on the road.

stories.title_en: Taking Bleached Fake Silver at the Maozhou Fair

paragraphs.zh: 钱天广，福建安海人也。时买机布，往山东冒州药王会卖。会期四月十五日起，二十五日止。天下货物，咸在斯处交卸。无牙折中，贸易二家自处。
paragraphs.en: Qian Tianguang was a man of Anhai in Fujian. At the time he bought loom cloth and went to sell it at the Medicine King Fair in Maozhou, Shandong. The fair ran from the fifteenth of the fourth month to the twenty-fifth. Goods from all under heaven were delivered and sold there. There were no brokers to mediate; the two sides dealt on their own.

paragraphs.zh: 一棍以漂白银来买布。每五两一锭，内以真银，如假银一般，色同一样。棍将丝银先对。广以铁槌凿打，并无异样。打至十餘锭，通是一色。广说：“不须再凿槌打。”棍遂以漂白出对，共银六百餘两，内只有细丝银一百餘两，餘者皆假也。银交完讫，布搬去了。广收其银，检束行李，与乡里即雇骡车，直到临清，去买回头货物。取出其银，皆假银也。那时虽悔不及，然广不甚动情，只说云“是我方承得此会，他人出外贸易，从此止矣。”人慨斯人量大，有此大跌，后必有大发也。棍虽脱骗得金数百，然天理昭昭，子孙必不昌隆。盖假银天下处处有之，故录此以为后人之提防，勿蹈天广之覆辙也。按：棍之用假银，此为商者最难提防，必得其梗概，方能辨认。余于壬子秋，在书坊检得一小本仔，辨说银之真假，甚是明白。故录之，以为江湖诸君览之，则假银若一入眼，灼然明白。略陈其一二于左：
paragraphs.en: A swindler came to buy cloth with “bleached” silver. Each ingot was five taels; inside it was genuine silver, made to look like the fake, the color all one. The swindler first matched with silk-thread silver. Guang took an iron hammer and chisel and struck: nothing looked wrong. He struck more than ten ingots; all were the same color. Guang said, “No need to chisel and hammer any more.” The swindler then brought out the bleached silver to match: more than six hundred taels in all, of which only a little over a hundred taels was fine silk-thread silver; the rest was all fake. The silver was paid, the cloth was carried off. Guang put away the silver, packed his bags, and with his townsmen hired a mule cart straight to Linqing to buy goods for the return trip. He took out the silver: all fake. By then regret was too late, but Guang did not take it much to heart. He only said, “It is my luck to have been able to attend this fair; as for other men going out to trade, from now on they should stop.” People sighed that he had a large mind; after such a fall he would surely rise far later. The swindler had cheated several hundred in gold, but Heaven’s principle is clear: his descendants will not prosper. Fake silver is found everywhere under heaven, so I record this as a warning for those who come after, not to follow Qian Tianguang’s ruts. Note: A swindler’s use of fake silver is what merchants find hardest to guard against; you must have the general picture before you can tell it. In the autumn of the renzi year I found a little booklet in a bookshop that explained true and fake silver very clearly. I copy it here for gentlemen of the rivers and lakes to read, so that once fake silver meets the eye it is obvious. I set out a little of it below:

paragraphs.zh: 夫元宝者，坑淘出而原宝。今之官解钱粮，亦倾煎如坑淘出厚色，而成元宝也。俗云“圆宝”是也。
paragraphs.en: Yuanbao: the “original treasure” washed from the pits. Today official shipments of tax silver are also melted and refined to the thick color of pit-washed silver and made into yuanbao. Commonly called “round treasure.”

paragraphs.zh: 松纹，与细丝一样，其皆足色也。
paragraphs.en: Pine-grain (songwen) is the same as fine-thread (xisi); both are full-color, pure silver.

paragraphs.zh: 摇丝，色未甚足。银泻入，以手摇动而成丝也，曰摇丝。
paragraphs.en: Shaken-thread (yaosi): the color is not yet quite full. When the silver is poured in, it is shaken by hand to form threads; hence “shaken-thread.”

paragraphs.zh: 水丝，又名曰干丝，自七成、八成、九成、九五止，通名曰水丝。
paragraphs.en: Water-thread (shuisi), also called dry-thread (gansi): from seven-tenths, eight-tenths, nine-tenths, up to nine-and-a-half tenths, all are called water-thread.

paragraphs.zh: 画丝，即水丝。泻出而无丝，以铁锥画丝于其上，曰画丝。
paragraphs.en: Drawn-thread (huasi) is water-thread. It is poured with no thread; an iron awl is used to draw threads on the surface; hence “drawn-thread.”

paragraphs.zh: 吹丝，即九程水丝。银一入，口含吹筒即吹之以成丝也，曰吹丝。
paragraphs.en: Blown-thread (chuisi) is nine-tenths water-thread. As soon as the silver goes in, a blowpipe is held in the mouth and it is blown to form threads; hence “blown-thread.”

paragraphs.zh: 吸丝，以湿纸盖其上，中取一孔，以银从孔泻下，吸以成其丝也，曰吸丝。今人以铁箔盖于上，亦中取一孔，银从孔泻下，亦吸以成丝也。盖吸丝自七成起，九五止。九五者，亦看得足色也。
paragraphs.en: Sucked-thread (xisi): wet paper is laid over the top, a hole is made in the middle, silver is poured through the hole, and it is sucked into threads; hence “sucked-thread.” Today people use an iron foil on top, likewise with a hole in the middle; silver poured through is also sucked into threads. Sucked-thread runs from seven-tenths up to nine-and-a-half. The nine-and-a-half can also pass for full color.

paragraphs.zh: 茶花，以纹银九钱，入铅一钱，入炉中锅内不用一毫之硝，明倾取出，以把淡底填于脚。后泻银于内，铅方不露，而自成其粗丝也，曰茶花。
paragraphs.en: Tea-flower (chahua): take nine qian of fine silver and one qian of lead, put them in the furnace pan with not a scrap of niter, pour it out openly, pack a pale base into the “feet,” then pour the silver in so the lead does not show, and coarse threads form of themselves; hence “tea-flower.”

paragraphs.zh: 鼎银，即汞银也，又曰水银。以纹银五钱，以汞五钱半，入铁鼎中，倾其色通红于内，取出候冷，拿出其银，止有一两，拆汞五分，可打之而成，或造之以成饼。以银薄贴于外，以墨微洒之，以掩其太白。更能造酒器，及诸项首饰。能拔银丝，亦犹细丝者，只是色略青些。更有赤脚汞银，文银三钱，铜丝二钱，汞五钱半，如同前，倾煎取出，不能打造，亦如同水丝一般。若辨汞银，其色脚嫩，上面银薄贴，色不同赤脚者。然色赤而带嫩，终不如水丝色老。此上古所传。造此换人，亦发家数千。子孙继迹不肖，而家即萧条。害众成家，终不悠久。
paragraphs.en: Tripod silver (dingyin) is mercury silver, also called quicksilver. Take five qian of fine silver and five and a half qian of mercury, put them in an iron tripod, pour until the color inside is all red, take it out, let it cool, and remove the silver: you get only one tael, losing five fen of mercury. It can be beaten into shape or made into cakes. Silver leaf is pasted on the outside and a little ink is sprinkled to hide the too-white color. It can also be made into wine vessels and all kinds of ornaments. It can be drawn into silver wire, still like fine-thread, only a little greener in color. There is also “bare-foot” mercury silver: three qian of fine silver, two qian of copper wire, five and a half qian of mercury; treated as above, poured and refined and taken out. It cannot be worked, and is like water-thread. To tell mercury silver: the color of the feet is tender; the silver leaf pasted on top does not match the color of the bare-foot kind. The color is red yet tender, and in the end not as aged as water-thread. This is what was handed down from ancient times. Those who made it to swap on people also built up thousands for their houses. When descendants followed the trade and were no good, the house at once fell thin. Harming the many to build a house does not last.

paragraphs.zh: 铜，以铜嵌四旁，而后以银泻下，藏其铜于中，曰铜。辨之虽看其丝，终不如细丝之明。其丝粗而带滞碍，即可疑而凿之，方露其铜。
paragraphs.en: Copper (tong): copper is set in on four sides, then silver is poured down, hiding the copper in the middle; this is called “copper.” Even if you look at the threads, they are never as clear as fine-thread. The threads are coarse and catch; that is enough to raise suspicion, and when you chisel, the copper shows.

paragraphs.zh: 铁碎，以铁碎先放于内，然后以银泻诸，适均入其银内，包藏铁于其中。至低者亦有九成，九五者有丝。
paragraphs.en: Iron-bits (tiesui): broken iron is first placed inside, then silver is poured so that it is evenly taken into the silver, wrapping the iron in the middle. The lowest still has nine-tenths; the nine-and-a-half has threads.

paragraphs.zh: 或以铜碎如前，名曰包销银。至低者亦有九成；九五有丝，九成无丝。
paragraphs.en: Or copper bits are used in the same way; this is called wrapped-solder silver (baoxiao). The lowest still has nine-tenths. Nine-and-a-half has threads; nine-tenths has none.

paragraphs.zh: 钞仔铜，用铜一两，入银三分，入炉中。以白信石如硝抽入，泻入中。取出铗四旁者三四分重片，中心者又入炉中倾。再铗，如此者数次。然后用银末，以碗极细，用酸砒草捣汁，入硼砂三分，以罐仔同煮。后放前银末三分，入砒草汁内。以前铜入罐中，以筋炒之，取出，以白水洗去其砒草汁，其色甚白。有一人问曰：“铜中只用银三分，后又以银末三分，何能使银相交于外？”其人对曰：“世间宝物，惟金银为至宝。若先不以银三分入铜倾煎，则后用银末亦为煎煮，必不能入。先以银三分入内，则后用此银末煮之，自然相应也。”故造假银，俗曰“神仙”。然辨此铜，当认银色，乃死鱼白，无青白之色。再看其脚，有两样：或用胭脂点，或用石点。须在点脚及死鱼白处辨之处，则真、赝了然。
paragraphs.en: Chaozai copper: take one tael of copper and three fen of silver into the furnace. White arsenolite, used like niter, is drawn in and poured into the middle. Take it out and clip from the four sides pieces of three or four fen; the center goes back into the furnace to be poured again. Clip again, several times like this. Then take silver powder, grind it extremely fine in a bowl, pound sour-arsenic grass for juice, add three fen of borax, and boil together in a small jar. After that put in the former three fen of silver powder in the grass juice. Put the copper into the jar, stir with chopsticks, take it out, and wash off the grass juice with clear water: the color is very white. Someone asked, “You use only three fen of silver in the copper, then another three fen of silver powder—how can the silver join on the outside?” The answer: “Of the world’s treasures, only gold and silver are the supreme treasures. If you do not first put three fen of silver into the copper and melt it, then later when you boil with silver powder it still will not go in. First put three fen of silver inside, then boil with this silver powder, and they answer each other of themselves.” So making fake silver is commonly called “the immortals’ art.” To tell this copper, look at the silver color: it is dead-fish white, with no blue-white. Look again at the feet: there are two kinds—either spotted with rouge, or spotted with mineral pigment. You must tell it at the spotted feet and the dead-fish white; then true and false are obvious.

paragraphs.zh: 漂白，用银倾煎细丝一样，只是甚热而壁乃薄，而后以，去其下面者，只留上面其薄者，中以白铜倾一无壁，以前上面安于其上，下面用银箔合其下，用焊焊之。后用滓槌槌其脚，为风锅无二。虽以凿凿开，必不能辨。如辨此，则当时烧焊之际，以火烧去其青青自然之色，如死鱼之白，故曰漂白。以此辨之，灼然明白矣。
paragraphs.en: Bleached (piaobai): silver is poured and refined just like fine-thread, only it is very hot and the walls are thin. Then the underside is taken away, leaving only the thin top. White copper is poured in the middle with no wall of its own; the former top is set on it, silver foil is joined underneath, and it is soldered. Then a dross-hammer is used on the feet, no different from a wind-pot. Even if you chisel it open you still may not tell. To identify it: at the time of soldering, fire burns away the natural bluish color, leaving a dead-fish white; hence “bleached.” Tell it this way, and it is perfectly clear.

paragraphs.zh: 煎饼银法，每铅一钱，销铜一分。若九成银一两，可用铅一两；八成可用铅二两，七成可用铅三两，灰堤中用炭装炉，慢扇其火，煎至铅化。若过后，必急扇其火，待油珠大如豆者，即以盖盖之，煞出止九五色。如待金花灿烂，煞出即结布于上，曰布心饼，又曰焦心饼。下面蟹眼回珠，二面皆白，即松纹足色。
paragraphs.en: Method for refined-cake silver: for every qian of lead, melt one fen of copper. For one tael of nine-tenths silver you may use one tael of lead; eight-tenths may use two taels of lead; seven-tenths may use three taels. In an ash dike, load charcoal in the furnace, fan the fire slowly, and refine until the lead melts. After that you must fan hard. When the oil beads are as large as beans, cover it. If you take it out then, it stops at nine-and-a-half color. If you wait until golden flowers blaze, then take it out, a crust forms on top, called cloth-heart cake, also scorched-heart cake. Below, crab-eye returning pearls; both faces white: that is pine-grain full color.

paragraphs.zh: 九成饼，亦出炉白。上乃鸡爪面，下面脚亦白。
paragraphs.en: Nine-tenths cake also comes from the furnace white. The top is a chicken-claw face; the feet below are also white.

paragraphs.zh: 八成饼，出炉略黑，必用天砂擦之方白。上面蚤斑之痕，剪开略白。
paragraphs.en: Eight-tenths cake comes from the furnace a little black; you must rub it with heaven-sand before it is white. There are flea-spot marks on top; when you snip it open it is a little white.

paragraphs.zh: 七成饼，出炉墨黑，亦用砂擦及用盐梅洗之方白，其剪口带赤。
paragraphs.en: Seven-tenths cake comes from the furnace ink-black; you also rub it with sand and wash it with salted plums before it is white; the snipped mouth has a reddish tinge.

paragraphs.zh: 六成比七成犹不同些。
paragraphs.en: Six-tenths differs a little further from seven-tenths.

paragraphs.zh: 五成即梅白饼。
paragraphs.en: Five-tenths is the plum-white cake.

paragraphs.zh: 盐烧饼，二钱五分银出一两，取出以盐烂水，调上一重在其饼上，入火烧之，取出以锤打去一重铜皮；又用盐烧之，再锤打。如此者数次，则外面铜去而自然白，曰盐烧。
paragraphs.en: Salt-burned cake: two qian five fen of silver yields one tael. Take it out, mix rotten salt water, spread a layer on the cake, put it in the fire, take it out, and hammer off a layer of copper skin; salt-burn again, hammer again. Several times like this, and the outer copper goes and it turns white of itself; this is called salt-burn.

paragraphs.zh: 白铜倾者即白盐烧。
paragraphs.en: What is poured from white copper is white salt-burn.

paragraphs.zh: 三铗饼，底是足色饼，用如纸薄，中用白饼熔一饼于中。上面用银入炉中倾出细丝，入铅二三钱，取出，泻入炭锅，成一饼样，亦用甚薄，盖于其上。然后用焊焊成一饼，铗去其四旁者，中间的饼对面剪铗，尽可瞒人。辨之其饼厚，上下皆真银，中间色目异样。知者以银面于杉木擦之，即见三样色。
paragraphs.en: Three-clip cake: the bottom is a full-color cake, thin as paper; in the middle a white cake is melted in; on top, silver is put in the furnace, poured as fine-thread, two or three qian of lead added, taken out, poured into a charcoal pan into cake shape, also very thin, and laid over the top. Then it is soldered into one cake. The four sides are clipped away; if you snip and clip the middle cake face to face, it can quite take people in. To tell it: the cake is thick; top and bottom are true silver, the middle a different color. Those who know rub the silver face on fir wood, and three colors appear at once.

paragraphs.zh: 车壳即灌铅，以松纹细丝面，以落锥落一孔，然后以割仔入其内割之，尽取其囊中者，留其银壳。后用铅灌其内填满，再用银打一尖仔尖之，又以铁錾仔錾之，如风锅一般。然辨此银，要看其两面之痕处，即见明白。
paragraphs.en: Turned-shell (cheke) is lead-filled. On a pine-grain fine-thread face, a dropping-awl makes a hole; then a cutter is put in and the inside is cut away, emptying the pouch and leaving the silver shell. Lead is then poured in to fill it; a silver point is beaten and plugged in; an iron chisel works it over, like a wind-pot. To tell this silver, look at the marks on both faces, and it is clear.

paragraphs.zh: 倒茅饼，先以上号白信石，用熔成罐不洧水者，以盐泥固济，入信石于内。打二炷香升灯盏上，轻清者听用。以银七钱、铜三钱五分熔。将起炉时，以前信石七分入银内，将盖盖之。取出天砂擦之，其面上亦鸡爪面，如九成银一般。辨之九成出炉自白，不待砂擦；然此饼铗口带黄，九成饼铗口自白。以此辨之朗然。
paragraphs.en: Inverted-thatch cake (daomao): first take top-grade white arsenolite, melt it in a jar that will not take water, seal with salt mud, put the arsenolite inside. Burn two sticks of incense under a lamp-dish; keep the light, clear part for use. Melt seven qian of silver and three qian five fen of copper. As you are about to take it from the furnace, put seven fen of the former arsenolite into the silver and cover it. Take it out and rub with heaven-sand; the face also has chicken-claw marks, like nine-tenths silver. To tell it: nine-tenths comes from the furnace white of itself and needs no sand-rubbing; but this cake’s clipped mouth has a yellow tinge, while a nine-tenths cake’s clipped mouth is white of itself. Tell it this way and it is plain.

paragraphs.zh: 更有铁线饼、江山白、华光桥、神仙饼、糁铜饼、倒插铅，其餘奇巧假银数十样，非言语笔舌所能形容。知者引申触类，观此思过半矣。有等游惰好闲、不务生理、受磨丧心、用此假银苟计衣食，以度时光，此犹穷徒，故不足责；然今贪黜之辈，家颇殷足，尚换此银，用以毒众，自图富厚，以遗子孙。不知丧心悖理，岂有善报，子孙其能昌乎！凡四民交易，止可用七成以至细丝，更低者不可用也。如昧心欺人，不唯阴遣之罪难偿，而阳报之网亦不漏矣。
paragraphs.en: There are also iron-wire cake, Jiangshan white, Huaguang Bridge, immortal cake, sprinkled-copper cake, inverted-inserted lead, and several dozen other ingenious fakes that speech and brush cannot describe. Those who know can extend the class from the instance; look at this and you have more than half. There are idlers who will not work at a living, who grind themselves down and lose all conscience, and use this fake silver as a makeshift for clothes and food to pass the time—poor wretches, not worth blaming. But now greedy, debased men, whose houses are already fairly well off, still swap this silver to poison the many, seeking wealth for themselves to leave to sons and grandsons. They do not know that those who lose conscience and go against principle have no good recompense; can their descendants flourish? In all dealings among the four classes of people, use only from seven-tenths up to fine-thread; anything lower must not be used. If you darken your heart to cheat others, not only is the unseen punishment hard to pay, the net of visible retribution will not miss you either.

stories.title_en: Overhearing the Official, Then Going Out to Swindle

paragraphs.zh: 里有寡婦，富蓋鄉鄰。止生一子甘澍，年方弱冠，恪守祖業，不敢生放。鄉人路五两問之借銀谷，皆不肯，心恨之。歸與妻胡氏謀，要賴他强姦。妻許曰：“可。”又托心友支九为干证，即往分巡道处告。道亲提审，先問胡氏曰：“甘澍因何到你家？”胡氏曰：“他家豪富，终日无图，只是姦淫人婦女。知我男人未在家，无故来调戏我；不从便强抱亲嘴，骂他不去。支九来邀我夫贩货，甘澍方走去。”再問支九：“你往路五家何干？”支九曰：“小的與路五都挑贩为生，因邀他买货，听得（里）面婦人喊骂，甘澍走出。”又問甘澍曰：“你因何與婦人角口？”甘澍曰：“并无到他家，哪有角口？問路五左右鄰便知。”左右鄰都称：“甘澍寡婦之子，素不敢非为。外间并未聞姦情，此是装情捏他。”路五执曰：“他万金巨富，岂不能买两个干证？”左右鄰曰：“我鄰近不知，他支九隔越一街，岂不是买来作证？”道曰：“路五贫民，何能买人作证？”将左右鄰并甘澍各责二十，定要問做强姦。甘澍出而惧甚，思无解释。
paragraphs.en: In the ward there was a widow, richer than the neighbors. She had only one son, Gan Shu, just of age, who kept to the family property and dared not lend at interest. A fellow villager, Lu Wu, asked him twice for a loan of silver and grain; both times he refused, and Lu hated him. Lu went home and plotted with his wife, née Hu, to frame Gan for rape. She agreed. He also enlisted a trusted friend, Zhi Jiu, as a witness, and they went to the circuit inspector’s office to file the charge. The inspector heard the case himself. He first asked Hu Shi, “Why did Gan Shu come to your house?” Hu Shi said, “His family is rich and idle all day; he only debauches other men’s women. He knew my husband was not at home, came for no reason to tease me; when I would not, he seized me and kissed me. I cursed him and he would not go. Zhi Jiu came to ask my husband to go trading, and only then did Gan Shu leave.” He asked Zhi Jiu, “What business had you at Lu Wu’s?” Zhi Jiu said, “I and Lu Wu both live by carrying goods to sell. I went to ask him to buy stock. I heard a woman inside shouting and cursing, and Gan Shu came out.” He asked Gan Shu, “Why did you quarrel with the woman?” Gan Shu said, “I never went to his house. How could there be a quarrel? Ask Lu Wu’s neighbors on either side and you will know.” The neighbors all said, “Gan Shu is a widow’s son and has never dared do wrong. We have heard of no adultery from outside; this is a cooked-up story to frame him.” Lu Wu insisted, “He is worth ten thousand in gold. How could he not buy two witnesses?” The neighbors said, “We live next door and know nothing. Zhi Jiu lives a street away. Is he not a bought witness?” The inspector said, “Lu Wu is a poor man. How could he buy witnesses?” He had the neighbors and Gan Shu each beaten twenty strokes, and was determined to convict rape. Gan Shu came out badly frightened, and could think of no way out.

paragraphs.zh: 晚堂退后，道已封门，在后堂周旋闲行，沉默思想，忽自言曰：“错矣！错矣！”又周行数次，遂拂衣而入。适有防夫涂山，在外窥道举动，聞其言错，想必是审此姦情一事也。夤夜越墙而出，扣甘澍歇家门。歇家开门延入。甘澍正忧闷无计。涂山曰：“你今日事要关节否？”澍曰：“甚关节可解？正要求之。”涂山曰：“道爷适有妻舅到，三日内即要打发起身，唯此最灵。若投他，明日即复审，更大胜矣。”澍曰：“如此得可好。须銀几何？”涂山曰：“此翻自案事，不比别人情，须百金方可。”澍曰：“百金我出，只要明日复审。”涂山曰：“舅爷今酒席尚未散，吾当即入言之。”澍與歇家送出。道大门已封，涂山复从居旁民家越墙而入。
paragraphs.en: After the evening session the inspector had already sealed the gates. He paced in the rear hall, thinking in silence, then suddenly said to himself, “Wrong! Wrong!” He walked around several more times, then shook out his sleeves and went in. It happened that a watchman, Tu Shan, was outside watching the inspector’s movements. Hearing him say “wrong,” he guessed it must be this rape case. In the dead of night he climbed the wall, went out, and knocked at the inn where Gan Shu was staying. The innkeeper opened and let him in. Gan Shu was sitting worried, with no plan. Tu Shan said, “For today’s business, do you want a private channel?” Shu said, “What channel would clear it? That is just what I need.” Tu Shan said, “His Honor the inspector happens to have a wife’s brother visiting. In three days he must be sent off. This is the most effective route. If you go through him, there will be a rehearing tomorrow, and you will win still more.” Shu said, “If that works, good. How much silver?” Tu Shan said, “This is a matter on his own docket, not like an ordinary favor. It will take a hundred taels.” Shu said, “I will put up a hundred taels, so long as there is a rehearing tomorrow.” Tu Shan said, “The uncle’s feast has not yet broken up. I will go in and speak at once.” Shu and the innkeeper saw him out. The inspector’s main gate was already sealed; Tu Shan again climbed the wall through a neighboring house and went in.

paragraphs.zh: 次日，道出早堂，即出牌复审强姦事。甘澍大喜，以为果验也。下午再审甘澍曰：“路五曾問你措借否？”澍曰：“他两次問借銀谷，我皆不肯，因此仇恨，妆情诬我。”再审胡氏曰：“甘澍未到你家，哪有强姦事？将拶起！”路五边未用銀，一拶即紧。胡氏难忍，即吐实“未有强姦。只措借不肯，故妆情告他。”又将路五、支九各打三十，将甘澍全解无罪。涂山即跟出索銀。甘澍曰：“吾乐與之。”涂山自索谢，澍另以十两與之。涂山以銀入道卸起，再出索添谢，又得十两。当时以舅爷关节之力，岂知出道之自悔，而銀尽为涂山所风騙乎！
paragraphs.en: The next day the inspector held morning court and at once issued a slip for a rehearing of the rape case. Gan Shu was overjoyed, thinking it had indeed taken effect. In the afternoon Gan Shu was examined again: “Did Lu Wu ever press you for a loan?” Shu said, “Twice he asked to borrow silver and grain; I refused both times. That is why he hates me and cooked up this charge.” Hu Shi was examined again: “Gan Shu never came to your house. How could there be a rape? Bring the finger-squeezers!” Lu Wu’s side had spent no silver; the squeezers were tightened at once. Hu Shi could not bear it and told the truth: “There was no rape. He would not lend, so we cooked up a charge.” Lu Wu and Zhi Jiu were each given thirty strokes, and Gan Shu was fully cleared as not guilty. Tu Shan followed him out to demand the silver. Gan Shu said, “I am glad to give it.” Tu Shan took his own thank-you; Shu gave him another ten taels besides. Tu Shan took the silver into the yamen, put it away, came out again to demand more thanks, and got another ten taels. At the time they thought it was the power of the uncle’s private channel. How were they to know it came from the inspector’s own second thoughts, and that all the silver had been pocketed by Tu Shan as a windfall swindle?

paragraphs.zh: 按：衙役皆以騙养身供家，丰衣足食，其騙何可枚举！蓋事事是騙，日日是騙，人人是騙。虽罄南山竹，何能悉之；虽包拯再生，何能察之？予素不入公庭，此中情弊，希所知聞。此其偶得于真见者，故述其弊窦如此。然衙中虽人人是姦徒，事事是騙薮，吾唯早完公课，百忍不讼，虽贪吏悍卒，其如我何！故曰：机虽巧，不蹈为高；鸩虽毒，不饮为高；衙役虽騙，不入为高。纵有无妄之灾，必有明官能昭雪之者。何也？官皆读书人，明者多而昏者少也。无奈在衙人役，各以阴云霾雾蔽之耳。故唯忍小忿，不入衙为高也。
paragraphs.en: Note: Yamen runners all live by swindling, to keep their families in ample clothes and food. How can their swindles be counted one by one? For every affair is a swindle, every day is a swindle, every person is a swindle. Even if you used up the bamboos of the southern hills, you could not set them all down; even if Bao Zheng were born again, he could not see through them. I have never been one to enter a public court; of the tricks inside I have heard little. This I happened to see for myself, so I record the opening as it was. Yet though every man in a yamen is a knave and every affair a nest of swindles, if I only pay my public dues early and endure a hundred wrongs rather than sue, then greedy clerks and fierce soldiers can do nothing to me. So it is said: a trap may be clever—the high thing is not to step in it; a poison may be deadly—the high thing is not to drink it; yamen runners may swindle—the high thing is not to go in. Even if some undeserved disaster comes, there will surely be a clear-eyed official to right it. Why? Officials are all men who have read books; the clear ones are many and the muddled few. The trouble is only that the men serving in the yamen screen them with dark cloud and fog. So the high thing is to swallow small anger and not enter a yamen.

stories.title_en: Drafting a Heavy Sentence on Purpose to Free a Prisoner

paragraphs.zh: 富民元植者，家温行谨，奕世良善，偶與鄉权贵有隙。鄉贵素善叶推官，乃吹毛求疵，砌元植之恶十餘件。叶推官为之送访，按院即批與叶审。叶提元植，谕之曰：“汝之恶迹，我已备晓，罪在有定。只汝家殷富，不許央关节。若有关节，罪有加无减。且收入监，候拘到被害，即听审定罪。”叶推官素廉正，从来不纳分上。今元植既承面诫，越不敢展转，只惶惧待罪耳。
paragraphs.en: A well-off commoner named Yuan Zhi was comfortable in his means and careful in his conduct, of a line of decent people for generations. He happened to have a quarrel with a powerful man of the district. That man had long been on good terms with Assistant Prefect Ye, so he picked bones and piled up more than ten charges of Yuan Zhi’s “evils.” Assistant Prefect Ye sent them up as an investigation; the touring censor then assigned the case to Ye. Ye had Yuan Zhi brought in and told him, “I already know your misdeeds in full; the punishment is fixed. Your family is rich: you are not to send private appeals. If there is a private appeal, the punishment will be increased, not reduced. Put him in jail. When the alleged victims have been summoned, we will hear the case and pass sentence.” Assistant Prefect Ye had always been honest and never took a word from anyone. Yuan Zhi, having been warned to his face, still less dared to stir, and only waited in fear for punishment.

paragraphs.zh: 适眷亲易鄉官，素與植相善，知其事属仇陷，默地代诉于太府，托转释于四尊。太府乘间缓颊及之。叶四尊大怒，歸取元植，责之曰：“我叫你不得投分上，反央太爷来讲。这样刁恶人，定要拟你谪戍！”元植茫不知来历，叩头曰：“老爷素不纳关节，一府通知；又蒙钧旨面谕，怎敢央太爷？实不知事从何来。”叶爷曰：“且入监去，定是军罪。”元植出查，方知事出易鄉官，自以己意代释，并不使植知也。植思无处可解，寻其用事凌书手，密商曰：“能为我减军入徒，当以厚礼谢。”凌书曰：“能出百金，为汝计之。”植許曰：“可。”以銀封讫。
paragraphs.en: It happened that a kinsman, retired official Yi, had long been friendly with Zhi. Knowing the matter was an enemy’s trap, he quietly spoke for him to the prefect, asking the prefect to pass a word to the Fourth Lord (Ye) for a release. The prefect found an opening and eased the matter along. Fourth Lord Ye was furious. He had Yuan Zhi brought back and rebuked him: “I told you not to send in a word, and you instead got His Honor the prefect to speak. A vicious man like you—I am determined to sentence you to frontier military exile!” Yuan Zhi had no idea where this had come from. He kowtowed: “Your Honor never takes private channels; the whole prefecture knows it. And I was ordered to my face. How would I dare send the prefect? I truly do not know how this arose.” Lord Ye said, “Go back into jail. It will certainly be a military sentence.” Yuan Zhi came out and inquired, and only then learned it had come from retired official Yi, who of his own accord had spoken for a release without letting Zhi know. Zhi could think of no way out. He sought out Ling, the clerk who handled the work, and said in private, “If you can get my military exile reduced to penal servitude, I will thank you richly.” Clerk Ling said, “If you can put up a hundred taels, I will manage it for you.” Zhi agreed, and sealed up the silver.

paragraphs.zh: 叶爷果唤凌书手作招曰：“须寻一军律拟来。”凌书故以绞罪拟上。叶爷命改招，只可拟军。凌书过一日再以绞罪拟曰：“访单中惟謀死亲弟一件最重，正合绞罪。餘某条某条，只是徒罪，并无合军律者。”叶爷寻思：“有对头之状，尚不轻入人绞，况是拿访，而可绞人？”曰：“造化了他，只拟徒罢。”后拟上三年徒。元植欣然纳赎，凌书遂安受百金之贿。在叶爷，宁知其外受金而内拟人重罪乎？故衙役之欺官，虽神君不及察也。
paragraphs.en: Lord Ye did in fact call Clerk Ling to draft the confession-and-sentence: “Find a military statute and propose it.” Ling deliberately proposed strangulation. Lord Ye ordered the draft changed: only military exile could be proposed. A day later Ling again proposed strangulation: “On the investigation list, the heaviest item is plotting the death of a younger brother, which exactly fits strangulation. The other articles are only penal servitude; none fits a military statute.” Lord Ye thought: “Even on a complaint from an enemy I would not lightly send a man to the silk cord; still less on a picked-up investigation.” He said, “His luck. Just propose penal servitude.” In the end it was three years’ servitude. Yuan Zhi gladly paid the redemption; Clerk Ling quietly took the hundred-tael bribe. As for Lord Ye, how was he to know that outside someone had taken gold, and inside a heavier crime had been proposed against the man? So when yamen clerks cheat an official, even a spirit-like magistrate cannot see it.

paragraphs.zh: 按：善有旌奖，恶有拿访，此朝廷激劝一大机权也。今旌者多由攒刺之巧，访者或由权贵之嗾，其虚实益相半耳。然犹幸有拿访一途，可以少惕刁顽，稍为良民吐气。特被访者出入于問官之心，高下于权书之手，其情得罪当者亦少矣。当官持权者，或遇大故重情，必虚心详审，明察沉断，庶可杜姦欺之一二耳。
paragraphs.en: Note: The good are commended, the bad are seized and investigated: this is a great engine of the court for urging and warning. Today those commended often get there by clever self-promotion, and those investigated are sometimes set on by the powerful; truth and falsehood are about half and half. Still we are lucky to have investigation at all, which can somewhat cow the cunning and let decent people breathe a little. Only, those investigated rise and fall in the examining official’s mind and are raised or lowered in the powerful clerk’s hand; few in fact get the punishment they deserve. Those who hold office and wield power, when they meet a grave matter with heavy consequences, must empty their minds, examine in detail, look clearly and decide firmly; only then can they block one or two of the frauds.

stories.title_en: A Clerk Scolds a Convict in Order to Split the Beating

paragraphs.zh: 传包孝肃为官，清廉明察，用法无私，诈不得以巧辨售，罪不得以权贵免，又不纳分上。故人称之曰：“关节不到，有阎罗包老。”
paragraphs.en: It is told that when Bao Xiaosu was in office he was clean, clear-eyed, and used the law without private feeling. Trickery could not sell itself by clever argument; punishment could not be escaped by powerful connections; and he took no private word. So people said of him, “Where no private channel can reach, there is Yama Bao.”

paragraphs.zh: 适有富豪子犯姦情真，知难逃洞察，预與一老胥謀曰：“包爷精明，察事如神。我所犯情真，干证又直证，罪实难逃。若重罚犹可输纳；唯痛责实是难堪。有何计可以减责，必不惜厚费图之。”老胥曰：“明日若当责时，你奔近案前，强辩求申。我从旁呵斥，为你分责，或可减你一半。此外，别无策可图也。”
paragraphs.en: A rich man’s son was truly guilty of an illicit affair. Knowing he could not escape the clear eye, he plotted in advance with an old clerk: “Lord Bao is sharp and sees a case like a spirit. What I did is true, and the witnesses testify straight; the punishment can hardly be avoided. A heavy fine I could still pay; only a painful beating would be hard to bear. If there is any plan to reduce the beating, I will not begrudge a thick fee to work it.” The old clerk said, “Tomorrow, when the beating is due, run up to the bench and argue hard for a hearing. I will shout you down from the side and take part of the beating for you; perhaps your half can be cut. Beyond that there is no plan.”

paragraphs.zh: 次日，包公审得真情，发怒要打富子四十。富子奔近案（前），哓哓申辩不已。老胥从旁大声呵之曰：“速去受责，何须許多说话，罪岂赦你！”包公见之，大恨此吏揽权起威，恐后日窃势騙人，外必生事，即先责老胥二十板，偏减去富子二十，欲使威不自胥出，不知正落其謀中也。老胥遂得厚赂，而包公漠不知之。
paragraphs.en: The next day Lord Bao found the facts true, grew angry, and was going to give the rich son forty strokes. The rich son ran up to the bench and argued on and on. The old clerk shouted loudly from the side, “Go and take your beating at once! Why so much talk? Will the punishment be remitted for you?” Lord Bao saw this and hated the clerk for seizing power and putting on airs. He feared that later the man would steal influence to swindle people and make trouble outside, so he first beat the old clerk twenty strokes and, of all things, took twenty off the rich son, wanting the awe not to seem to come from the clerk—not knowing he had fallen right into the plot. The old clerk then got a thick bribe, and Lord Bao knew nothing of it.

paragraphs.zh: 按：吏为姦，皆是知本官性情，而变幻用之。老胥知包公严明，岂容胥吏招权？故旁呵犯人，包公必责吏而故恕犯人，以见胥吏之无权，欲外人不畏慑之。岂知于难减责之中，故分责以取其贿，又孰从而察之？公且受胥騙，况后之为官者哉！
paragraphs.en: Note: When clerks work fraud, they all know their superior’s temper and twist it to use. The old clerk knew Lord Bao was strict and clear, and would never let a clerk gather power. So he shouted at the prisoner from the side: Lord Bao was bound to beat the clerk and deliberately spare the prisoner, to show that clerks have no power, and so that people outside would not stand in awe of them. Who would have thought that, in a beating that could hardly be reduced, he would split the beating in order to take a bribe—and who would see through it? Even his lordship was swindled by a clerk; how much more those who hold office after him!

stories.title_en: A Woman Marries a Street Scavenger and Takes His Life

paragraphs.zh: 京城有房八者，为人痴蠢，以淘街为生，家止一老母。一日，房八淘街，往小河边洗。靠晚来有一妇人，身穿麻衣，旁立看淘洗讫，谓房八曰：“我将往娘家，今晚不能到，暂借你家一歇。”房八曰：“我家歇不得，何不往客店歇？”妇人曰：“客店人丛杂，（住）宿不便。你家有何人？”房八曰：“家有老母。”妇人曰：“有母便可同歇。”
paragraphs.en: In the capital there was a Fang Ba, a dull-witted man who lived by scavenging the streets. His household was only an old mother. One day Fang Ba was scavenging, then went to a small river to wash. Toward evening a woman in hemp mourning clothes stood by, watched him finish washing, and said, “I am going to my mother’s house. I cannot get there tonight. Let me rest a night at yours.” Fang Ba said, “My house is no place to stay. Why not an inn?” The woman said, “Inns are crowded; lodging is inconvenient. Who is in your house?” Fang Ba said, “I have an old mother.” The woman said, “If there is a mother, we can stay together.”

paragraphs.zh: 房八引至家，妇人把银与籴米买酒菜，夜间三人同食。妇人问：“曾娶媳否？”房母答：“家下仅能度日，哪得银娶媳？”妇人曰：“我前夫死已葬讫，家无亲人。今收拾家财，将回娘家，奈娘家又远。看你儿子孝善，偶然相遇，亦似天缘，意欲为你媳妇，以供奉朝夕，何如？”房母曰：“你虽好意，只恐儿不能供三口人。”妇曰：“我亦带有些少银本，谅勤治女工，亦足自给。”房八喜曰：“我算命今年当招好妻。一人自有一人禄，何患不能供？”是晚，遂成亲同宿。一夜之间，叙尽风流。男称前未娶，今如渴而得浆；女称久失偶，今如热而遇凉。二人交爱，真如鱼水。房母亦大喜天赐贤媳。
paragraphs.en: Fang Ba led her home. The woman gave silver for rice, wine, and dishes, and at night the three ate together. She asked, “Has he taken a wife?” The mother said, “We can barely get through the day. Where would we get silver for a daughter-in-law?” The woman said, “My former husband is dead and already buried. I have no kin at home. I have gathered the household goods to go back to my mother’s, but her house is far. I see your son is filial and kind. Meeting by chance seems Heaven’s match. I would like to be your daughter-in-law and serve you morning and night. How would that be?” The mother said, “You mean well, but I fear my son cannot feed three mouths.” The woman said, “I have also brought a little silver capital. If I work diligently at women’s work, it should be enough.” Fang Ba was pleased: “My fortune this year says I should get a good wife. Each person has each person’s allotted food. Why worry we cannot feed ourselves?” That night they became husband and wife and slept together. In one night they talked through all the tenderness of love. The man said he had never married, and now it was like thirst meeting drink; the woman said she had long been without a mate, and now it was like heat meeting cool. They loved each other truly like fish in water. The mother too was overjoyed at Heaven’s gift of a worthy daughter-in-law.

paragraphs.zh: 次日，妇以银六钱与夫籴米买菜蔬。第三日，问婆母曰：“何不做身衣服穿？”婆称无银。妇又出银六钱，叫夫在汪客大布店买之。房八既得妻，又前后得银作家，心中扬扬喜色，往汪店买青布二端归。妇各将剪去三尺，故持尺量曰：“此是剪剩之布，未成全匹。何被人瞒也？可持去与换。有好银买布，他何得如此亏人？”房八听妻言去换。汪店言：“我家哪有零布？是你自剪起胡赖我。”二人各争一场。汪客令家人再以二端与之。及持归，妇背地以剪刀刺破几叶，后将展开，又曰：“如何又换两匹碾烂布？这布店好可恶！他欺你纯善，故敢诳你。今次不换，可放言骂他，怕他什么！”房八被妻激，忿忿往说：“你以破布诳我。”汪客说：“你买一匹布，来换许多次，店中哪有此功夫！”不换与他。房八便纵言秽骂。汪客怒，喝令家人扯打一顿，后以两匹布打开看明，掷与之。房八执布归，言被打之恨。妻怒，顿足曰：“有银买布，反招他打。他靠财势，可拼命与他作对。吾与婆能替你申冤。”又激夫到店凶泼。汪店家人又群起痛打，带重伤而归。妇哭曰：“必往告保辜状。”遂往御史处告准。归买好酒好菜，劝夫多饮，方可散血。夫被其劝，酩酊大醉。夜乘醉，紧绑其手足，以沙塞口鼻，至三更死已久，解其绑绳。妇故喊曰：“你儿身冷了，硬了，莫非是死？”吓得婆起看，儿已死。二人相对哭尽哀，复往御史处补状。差官检验收贮，遍体都有重伤。汪客惊惶无措。
paragraphs.en: The next day the woman gave her husband six qian of silver to buy rice and vegetables. On the third day she asked her mother-in-law, “Why not have some clothes made to wear?” The old woman said she had no silver. The woman again put out six qian and told her husband to buy cloth at Wang the merchant’s large cloth shop. Fang Ba had got a wife and, before and after, silver to keep house; his face was full of high spirits. He went to Wang’s shop, bought two bolts of blue cloth, and came home. The woman cut three chi from each, then deliberately took a ruler and said, “This is leftover cut cloth, not a full bolt. How were we cheated? Take it back and exchange it. We paid good silver for cloth; how can they short us like this?” Fang Ba listened to his wife and went to exchange it. Wang’s shop said, “When did we ever have remnant cloth? You cut it yourself to cheat us.” The two argued. Wang told his men to give him two more bolts. When he brought them home, the woman, behind his back, stabbed several leaves with scissors, then spread them out and said again, “How is it you exchanged two more bolts of crushed, ruined cloth? This shop is hateful! They see you are simple, so they dare lie to you. This time if they will not exchange, curse them out loud. What is there to fear?” Fang Ba, stirred up by his wife, went in a rage and said, “You palmed broken cloth off on me.” Wang said, “You buy one bolt and come to exchange it many times. What shop has time for that?” He would not exchange. Fang Ba then let fly with filthy abuse. Wang grew angry, ordered his men to drag him and beat him, then opened the two bolts, looked them over, and threw them at him. Fang Ba took the cloth home and told of the beating with hate. The wife stamped her foot in anger: “We paid silver for cloth and instead got a beating. He leans on money and power. Risk your life against him. Your mother and I can plead your wrong.” She stirred her husband up again to go to the shop and make a scene. Wang’s household men rose together and beat him badly; he came home with heavy wounds. The woman wept: “We must file a bond to hold them for the injury.” She went to the censor and had the plaint accepted. Coming home she bought good wine and dishes, and urged her husband to drink much, so the blood would disperse. Urged by her, he got dead drunk. That night, while he was drunk, she bound his hands and feet tight, stuffed sand in his mouth and nose, and by the third watch he had long been dead. She untied the ropes. Then she deliberately cried, “Your son’s body is cold and stiff—can he be dead?” The frightened mother rose to look: her son was dead. The two wept together in full mourning, then went back to the censor to supplement the plaint. Officers examined and stored the body: there were heavy wounds all over. Wang the merchant was terrified and at a loss.

paragraphs.zh: 过三日将审，妇与婆到汪客店曰：“我夫被你打死已的，只我婆年老，我一妇人难独供膳，把你偿命亦无益。你能出银三百两，与我供奉婆婆，叫婆具息免检罢。”汪客闻言心喜，令人担议，许出银二百两，与房母养赡。房母依妇言，自具息言：“身贫老，儿死妇寡，莫能存命。凭亲邻劝谕，着汪出银一百两，与氏养赡，免行检验。”官准息，将汪客打二十，又罚一大罪，令房八妻领银而归。过两日，妇窃银二百两，夜间逃去，不知所往。房母再欲告，汪客又重出二十两与之，以息其事。
paragraphs.en: After three days, just before the hearing, the woman and the mother went to Wang’s shop and said, “My husband was beaten to death by you; that is certain. Only my mother-in-law is old, and I am one woman who can hardly feed us alone. If you pay with your life it does us no good. If you can put up three hundred taels for me to keep my mother-in-law, have her file a withdrawal and skip the inquest.” Wang heard this with a glad heart, sent people to bargain, and agreed to put up two hundred taels for Fang’s mother to live on. The mother, following the woman’s words, herself filed a withdrawal: “I am poor and old; my son is dead and the wife a widow; we cannot survive. By the urging of kin and neighbors, let Wang put up one hundred taels for my support, and waive the inquest.” The official allowed the withdrawal, had Wang given twenty strokes, fined him a large penalty besides, and had Fang Ba’s wife take the silver home. After two days the woman stole the two hundred taels and fled by night, no one knew where. The mother wanted to sue again; Wang put up another twenty taels to quiet the matter.

paragraphs.zh: 按：此妇是大棍之妻，查得房八止此老母，故遣妇假与为妻，激其与富店殴争，然后加力打死，则房母必告，必可得银，然后拐银而逃。是断送人一命，而彼得厚利也。世之奸险至此，人可痴心而犯其机阱乎！
paragraphs.en: Note: This woman was the wife of a master swindler. They had found that Fang Ba had only this old mother, so they sent the woman to pretend to be his wife, stirred him up to fight a rich shop, then used force to beat him to death. The mother would surely sue, they would surely get silver, then they would make off with the silver and flee. So they threw away a man’s life and took a thick profit. When the world’s treachery has come to this, can anyone still be simple-hearted enough to walk into the trap?

stories.title_en: A Matchmaker Tricks a Graduate into “Marrying” a Titled Lady

paragraphs.zh: 福建春元洪子选在京将纳妾，媒数引看，多未称意。适有崔命妇者，年近三十，犹绰约如处子。以为夫除服，入寺建醮。二棍套定，一为媒先引洪春元到寺亲看。洪见其容貌秀雅，言动庄重，大是快意。媒曰：“既称意，须与其大伯言之，此妇是伯主婚。”径引春元到其家，先袖钱五十文，入付其小家僮曰：“有一春元来尊府看大厦，托讨三杯茶与吃。”再出邀春元曰：“他大伯在外即回，可入厅坐。”少顷，一棍称为伯，从外入。三人叙礼，复坐，小仆捧茶出。媒曰：“令弟妇欲改造，此福建春元欲求娶，敬问礼银若干？”伯曰：“路太远些，恐弟妇外家不允。”媒曰：“他目今受官，即叫令弟舅同到任，亦何惮远？况他世家宦族，姻眷满朝，即在京亦多人看顾，此不可错过。但老爷尚未得见令弟妇。”伯笑曰：“舍弟妇人品德行女流第一，往日亦不肯令人见。今日除服，在某寺建醮，往彼处看之易矣。”媒曰：“尊府所出，亦不须看。但问何时肯去，及礼银若何？”伯曰：“她除服了，亦不拘时去。礼银须一百以上，她首饰妆奁，亦有五六十两。”旋引媒起，密曰：“我上贺须四十两，莫与弟妇知，其身资可减些。”再复入坐，复曰：“明日若交银，可在花园馆中。家中有俗忌，不交银也。”媒曰：“须请令弟舅同见为好。”伯曰：“彼来自多称说，待娶后即通未迟。”便送媒与春元出。媒曰：“适间伯与我言，须上贺银四十两，其身资可减些。彼不欲弟妇知，欲在园交银。”
paragraphs.en: Hong Zixuan, a Fujian graduate of the provincial examinations, was in the capital about to take a concubine. Matchmakers led him to look several times; most did not please him. There happened to be a titled lady of the Cui house, nearly thirty, still graceful as a girl. Thinking her mourning for her husband was over, she had gone into a temple to have rites performed. Two swindlers had it arranged: one, as matchmaker, first led Graduate Hong to the temple to look for himself. Hong saw that her looks were refined and her speech and bearing serious, and was greatly pleased. The matchmaker said, “Since she suits you, we must speak to her husband’s elder brother; this woman is given in marriage by the elder brother.” He led the graduate straight to the house, first tucked fifty cash in his sleeve, went in, and gave them to a young page: “A graduate has come to look at your fine residence; please ask for three cups of tea for him.” He came out again and invited the graduate: “Her elder brother-in-law is out and will be back at once. Come sit in the hall.” Shortly a swindler, posing as the elder brother, came in from outside. The three exchanged courtesy, sat again; the small servant brought tea. The matchmaker said, “Your younger brother’s wife wishes to remarry. This Fujian graduate seeks to take her, and respectfully asks how much betrothal silver.” The “elder brother” said, “The road is rather far; I fear her natal family will not agree.” The matchmaker said, “He will soon take office, and can have her brother go with him to the post; why fear the distance? Besides, he is of an official family for generations, with in-laws filling the court; even in the capital many will look after her. This must not be missed. Only his lordship has not yet seen your younger brother’s wife.” The elder brother smiled: “My younger brother’s wife is first among women in character and conduct, and in the past would not let people see her. Today her mourning is over; she is having rites at such-and-such a temple. To go there and look is easy.” The matchmaker said, “From a house like yours, there is no need to look. Only ask when she will go, and what the betrothal silver should be.” The elder brother said, “Her mourning is over; she can go anytime. The betrothal silver must be a hundred or more; her jewelry and trousseau are also worth fifty or sixty taels.” He then led the matchmaker aside and said privately, “My congratulatory gift must be forty taels; do not let my brother’s wife know. The body-price can be cut a little.” He sat down again and added, “If the silver is handed over tomorrow, do it in the garden lodge. There is a household taboo; we do not take silver in the house.” The matchmaker said, “Better invite her brother to meet as well.” The elder brother said, “If he comes he will talk too much. After the marriage it will not be too late to send word.” He then saw the matchmaker and the graduate out. The matchmaker said, “Just now the elder brother told me the congratulatory silver must be forty taels, and the body-price can be cut a little. He does not want his brother’s wife to know, and wants the silver handed over in the garden.”

paragraphs.zh: 次日，媒引春元及二管家同往园馆，又去邀崔家大伯同一小仆挟天平至。媒曰：“要叫一人写礼书。”伯曰：“亡弟未在，何用婚书？”媒曰：“京城交易，不比共府作事，只记一帐，亦有凭据。”伯曰：“吾自写何如？”媒曰：“最好。”即取纸与。写到财礼处，伯曰：“六十两。”媒曰：“减些，只四十。但要安顿令弟妇有好处，不必多索银。”伯曰：“两项可都一样。”媒曰：“易说的。”写完了，媒曰：“婚书放在我手，看对银。”先对四十两作一总封，又对二十两付与伯收。伯起曰：“吾取四十两，财礼任你家中面交；不然，亦不消说。”媒曰：“再加十两。”伯亦不肯。媒顾春元曰：“何如？”春元曰：“凑起四十两在你手，到他家交与妇人。”媒曰：“婚书并银，都要在我手，一同家中，两相交付。”伯曰：“我的非今日言明，要背交，昨已议定了。若事不成，岂能赖得？”媒惟取四十两并婚书在手，同春元回店，雇人去接亲。媒以婚书付春元曰：“事已定矣，不消带去。”只同两管家，领十餘人至崔家，先入厅旁坐。媒曰：“吾叫大伯来。”脱身去矣。
paragraphs.en: The next day the matchmaker led the graduate and two stewards to the garden lodge, and also went to invite the Cui “elder brother,” who came with a small servant carrying a balance. The matchmaker said, “We should call someone to write the betrothal letter.” The elder brother said, “My late brother is not here; what use is a marriage letter?” The matchmaker said, “A transaction in the capital is not like doing business in your own prefecture. Even a simple account is still evidence.” The elder brother said, “What if I write it myself?” The matchmaker said, “Best.” Paper was brought. When they came to the betrothal silver, the elder brother said, “Sixty taels.” The matchmaker said, “Cut it; only forty. Only settle your brother’s wife in a good place; no need to demand much silver.” The elder brother said, “The two sums can be the same.” The matchmaker said, “Easy to say.” When it was written, the matchmaker said, “Leave the marriage letter in my hand while we match the silver.” First they matched forty taels as one sealed packet, then matched twenty taels and gave them to the elder brother. The elder brother rose: “I will take the forty taels. The betrothal gift can be handed over at the house in her presence; otherwise there is nothing to discuss.” The matchmaker said, “Add another ten taels.” The elder brother would not. The matchmaker looked at the graduate: “What do you say?” The graduate said, “Make up forty taels in your hand, and at their house hand them to the woman.” The matchmaker said, “The marriage letter and the silver must both be in my hand; we go to the house together and both sides deliver.” The elder brother said, “Mine is not a matter of today’s talk; it was to be handed over behind her back, as we agreed yesterday. If the thing falls through, how could I keep it?” The matchmaker only took the forty taels and the marriage letter in hand, went back to the inn with the graduate, and hired men to fetch the bride. The matchmaker gave the marriage letter to the graduate and said, “The matter is settled; no need to take it along.” He went with only the two stewards and a dozen men to the Cui house and sat first at the side of the hall. The matchmaker said, “I will call the elder brother,” and slipped away.

paragraphs.zh: 崔家见许多人来，出问曰：“你辈何干？”管家对曰：“来接亲。”崔家人曰：“你走错门了，接甚亲？”管家曰：“媒人引我来，怎会错？”崔家人曰：“哪位是媒？”管家曰：“媒去叫你大伯。”崔家人曰：“有甚大伯？”管家曰：“是你家交银主婚的。”崔唾其面曰：“你一伙小辈该死的！此是崔爷府中，你信何人哄，在此胡说？”管家曰：“昨同洪相公在你家吃茶，许议亲事，已在花园交银了，今反退悔。我岂怕你的，难道脱得我银去？”崔家人曰：“谁把茶你吃，谁受你银？我家哪有出嫁的人？”管家曰：“你前日在寺中建醮的娘子要嫁。”崔家人曰：“啐！那是我主母，曾受朝廷诰命，谁人娶得！我去禀巡爷，把这伙棍徒锁去！”两管家见媒人请大伯不来，心中不安，各逃回店。崔家人尾其后，查是春元洪子选强婚，即往府尹告强娶命妇事。洪春元闻告，始知被棍脱，即逃出京去。及府尹差人来提，回报已无期走矣。府尹曰：“他自然要走，怎敢对得！”遂为立案存照，以俟后提。
paragraphs.en: The Cui household saw so many people coming and asked, “What is your business?” The stewards said, “We have come to fetch a bride.” The Cui people said, “You have the wrong door. What bride?” The stewards said, “The matchmaker led us. How could we be wrong?” The Cui people said, “Which of you is the matchmaker?” The stewards said, “The matchmaker went to call your elder brother-in-law.” The Cui people said, “What elder brother-in-law?” The stewards said, “The one in your house who took the silver and gives the bride in marriage.” The Cui people spat in their faces: “You pack of lowborns, you deserve to die! This is Lord Cui’s residence. Who fooled you into talking this nonsense here?” The stewards said, “Yesterday we drank tea in your house with Master Hong, agreed on a marriage, already handed over silver in the garden, and now you go back on it. Are we afraid of you? Can you make off with our silver?” The Cui people said, “Who gave you tea, who took your silver? Who in our house is to be married out?” The stewards said, “The lady who was having rites in the temple the other day wants to remarry.” The Cui people said, “Pah! That is our mistress, who holds an imperial patent of rank. Who can marry her! We will report to the patrol officer and have this pack of swindlers locked up!” The two stewards, seeing the matchmaker did not come back with the “elder brother,” grew uneasy and each fled to the inn. The Cui people followed, found it was Graduate Hong Zixuan forcing a marriage, and went to the prefect to charge him with forcibly marrying a titled lady. When Hong heard of the charge he knew he had been stripped by swindlers, and fled the capital. When the prefect sent men to bring him in, they reported he had already gone, no telling when. The prefect said, “Of course he would run. How would he dare face it!” So the case was filed for the record, to be taken up later.

paragraphs.zh: 按：此棍巧处，在见崔家主仆皆在寺，乃哄其家小仆进茶；又云大伯欲背索上贺，在园交银，故可行其骗。洪春元既失银，又着走。又府尹信其强娶，为之立案。在外娶妾，信然难哉！作事何可不审实也？
paragraphs.en: Note: The clever part of this swindle was seeing that the Cui master and servants were all at the temple, then tricking a young page of the house into serving tea; and saying the elder brother wanted a congratulatory gift in secret, with the silver handed over in the garden—that is how the cheat could be worked. Graduate Hong lost his silver and had to flee besides. And the prefect believed it was a forced marriage and filed the case. Taking a concubine away from home is truly hard! How can one act without checking the facts?

stories.title_en: Taking a Concubine in Another Province Brings a Lawsuit

paragraphs.zh: 广东蔡天寿者，为人慷慨仗义，年四十无子。其妻泼甚，弗容娶妾。一日，贩广锡三十餘担，往苏州府卖，与牙人萧汉卿曰：“我未得子，意欲在此娶一妾，亦有相因的否？”汉卿曰：“有银何怕无当意女子？”即领去看几个室女。汉卿曰：“我年过四十，此女皆年纪不相宜，吾不娶也。”
paragraphs.en: Cai Tianshou of Guangdong was open-handed and stood by his word. At forty he had no son. His wife was a shrew and would not let him take a concubine. One day he carried more than thirty loads of Guangdong tin to Suzhou to sell, and said to the broker Xiao Hanqing, “I have no son. I would like to take a concubine here. Is there anyone suitable?” Hanqing said, “If you have silver, why fear there is no girl to your liking?” He led him to look at several unmarried girls. Cai said, “I am past forty; these girls’ years do not match. I will not take them.”

paragraphs.zh: 忽有荡子国延纪，家有寡母邓氏，年三十三岁，容貌端好。夫死，遗家资千金，被延纪赌荡罄空，更欠赌银二十餘两，逼取无办。乃与棍商议，诈称母为妻，欲嫁以偿债。媒传于汉卿，领天寿看之，年貌合意，议身资银四十餘两。延纪曰：“氏系过江出身，恐外家阻挡，不与嫁远。其银可封牙人手，待临行上船，我叫人送到船来，人与银两相交付。”牙人以为可。
paragraphs.en: There happened to be a wastrel, Guo Yanji. His household had a widowed mother, née Deng, thirty-three, of decent looks. When her husband died he left a thousand taels; Yanji gambled it all away, and still owed more than twenty taels in gambling silver, which was being pressed with no way to pay. He plotted with swindlers to pass his mother off as his wife and marry her out to pay the debt. Word reached Hanqing through a matchmaker. He led Tianshou to look; age and looks suited, and they agreed on a body-price of a little over forty taels. Yanji said, “She comes from across the river. I fear her natal family will block it and not let her marry far. Seal the silver in the broker’s hand. When you are about to board, I will have her sent to the boat, and person and silver can be exchanged.” The broker thought this would do.

paragraphs.zh: 临行，延纪自雇轿，诈称母舅家接母。上船后，始知子将己脱嫁于客，心中甚怒，只忍气问曰：“夫既以我嫁人，何必相瞒，且娶我者是谁？”天寿应曰：“是不才。”妇曰：“看君谅是个富翁，我亦无恨。但我因夫赌荡，衣资首饰悉藏母家。我同你去取，亦且令母家得知。”天寿信之，与邓氏偕往。氏入诉其子背将己嫁之事。其兄邓天明发怒曰：“哪有子敢嫁母者！是何客人敢斗胆而娶？”出将天寿乱打。邓氏救止曰：“谅客人亦不知情，只不孝延纪，胆大该死！”天明即具状告县。邹爷准状，差拘延纪，逃走不出；先拘汉卿、天寿到。邹爷审出大怒，将婚主、媒人各责二十，以天寿收监，着汉卿讨延纪。数月，终不能拿，累被拿限拷打。天寿投分上释监，邹爷竟不许。人教天寿曰：“贼要贼拿，赌钱要赌钱人拿。何不许银与赌棍人拿？”不数日，贼指延纪所在，差人拿到。邹爷审出延纪以子嫁母与远客作妾，责四十板，拟重典，身资银追入官；汉卿、天寿各拟杖惩；其母取氏，着兄邓天明领归供养，任自择嫁，批照付之。
paragraphs.en: When it was time to leave, Yanji himself hired a sedan and pretended her mother’s brother’s house was fetching her. Only after she was on the boat did she learn her son had married her off to a traveling merchant. She was very angry, but swallowed it and asked, “Since my husband has married me off, why hide it? And who is taking me?” Tianshou answered, “This unworthy man.” The woman said, “You look to be a man of means; I have no hate. But because my husband gambled, my clothes, capital, and jewelry are all stored at my mother’s house. Come with me to fetch them, and also let my mother’s house know.” Tianshou believed her and went with Deng Shi. She went in and told how her son had married her off behind her back. Her elder brother Deng Tianming burst out: “Since when does a son dare marry off his mother! What traveling merchant has the gall to take her?” He came out and beat Tianshou wildly. Deng Shi stopped him: “I expect the guest did not know. It is only the unfilial Yanji who deserves to die for his daring!” Tianming filed a plaint at the county. Magistrate Zou accepted it, sent runners for Yanji, who fled and would not come out, and first had Hanqing and Tianshou brought in. Magistrate Zou, having heard the facts, was furious, beat the marriage-taker and the go-between twenty strokes each, put Tianshou in jail, and ordered Hanqing to produce Yanji. For several months they could not catch him; Hanqing was repeatedly summoned on deadline and beaten. Tianshou sent in a private word for release from jail; Magistrate Zou would not allow it. Someone taught Tianshou: “It takes a thief to catch a thief, a gambler to catch a gambler. Why not put up silver and have gambling swindlers seize him?” In a few days the thieves pointed out where Yanji was, and the runners brought him in. Magistrate Zou found that Yanji, a son, had married his mother off to a far-traveling guest as a concubine, gave him forty strokes, proposed a heavy statute, and had the body-price silver confiscated; Hanqing and Tianshou were each sentenced to the staff as a warning; the mother, Deng Shi, was given into her brother Deng Tianming’s care to support, free to choose another marriage, and a written order was issued to that effect.

paragraphs.zh: 按：为嗣娶妾，礼律不禁，特当娶于附近小户。若出外省，慕色而娶，多酿后患。若此类者，可为炯戒矣。
paragraphs.en: Note: Taking a concubine for the sake of an heir is not forbidden by ritual or statute. Only, one should take her from a nearby small household. If you go to another province and marry from lust for looks, you often brew later trouble. Cases of this kind may serve as a bright warning.

stories.title_en: A Frog Gives Away a Plot to Marry

paragraphs.zh: 徐州人陈彩，家资巨富，机智深密，有莽、操之奸。年三十岁，妻妾俱无子。邻舍潘，常借彩银，出外为商。彩往家，见其妻游氏美貌绝伦，遂起不良心。邀同本往瓜州买绵花，发广州等处卖。货收完，二人同归。路经西关渡，此幽僻之处，往来者稀。上渡，以篙撑船。彩暗忖：“此机可乘。”从后将一推落江。奔起水面，彩再以篙指落深渊。浸死之后，彩故叫渔翁捞其尸，以火焚之，裹骨归家。
paragraphs.en: Chen Cai of Xuzhou was enormously rich, deep and close in his schemes, with the treachery of a Mang or a Cao. At thirty, neither wife nor concubine had given him a son. A neighbor surnamed Pan often borrowed Chen Cai’s silver to go out trading. While Cai was at the Pan house he saw that Pan’s wife, née You, was unmatched in beauty, and an evil thought rose in him. He invited Pan to put in capital together, buy cotton at Guazhou, and sell it in Guangzhou and elsewhere. When the goods were sold they traveled home together. The road passed the West Gate ferry, a lonely place with few coming and going. They boarded, and a pole was used to push the boat. Cai thought in secret, “This chance can be used.” From behind he gave a shove and sent Pan into the river. When Pan broke the surface, Cai again used the pole to push him into the deep. After he had drowned, Cai deliberately called fishermen to drag up the body, had it burned, wrapped the bones, and went home.

paragraphs.zh: 彩穿白衣，见父母先大哭，而后报凶情。家大小都恸，乃细问身死因由。彩曰：“因过西关渡，上渡撑船，与篙并入水中。水深急，力不能起，遂致浸死。我雇人捞尸，焚骨而归。”言毕，潘家又哭。彩用将所卖帐薄并财本一一算明，交还之父母。满家反怀其德，哪知彩之设计谋死也。
paragraphs.en: Cai put on white mourning, saw the parents, first wept loudly, then reported the disaster. The whole household wailed, then asked in detail how he had died. Cai said, “Crossing at the West Gate ferry, he boarded and poled; he went into the water with the pole. The water was deep and swift; he had not the strength to rise, and so drowned. I hired men to recover the body, burned the bones, and came home.” When he had finished, the Pan house wept again. Cai then accounted for the sales ledger and the capital one by one and returned them to the parents. The whole family even felt grateful to him. How could they know Cai had plotted the death?

paragraphs.zh: 至半年后，父潘玉年老，有二幼孙不能抚养，欲以媳招人入赘，代理家事，与彩商议。彩曰：“入赘事久远，必得得当人方可；不然，家被他破害，后悔何及？依彩愚见，小心支持守节，勿嫁人为尚。”彩言虽如此，而中藏机械甚深。后有议入赘者，玉亦与彩议，彩皆设机破之。因先贿游氏之外家。
paragraphs.en: Half a year later the father, Pan Yu, was old, with two young grandsons he could not raise. He wanted to have his daughter-in-law take a man in as a live-in husband to manage the house, and discussed it with Cai. Cai said, “A live-in marriage is a long affair; you must get the right man. Otherwise he will break and harm the house, and regret will come too late. In my foolish view, the better course is to keep the household carefully and hold to widowhood, and not marry.” So Cai spoke, while the machinery he hid was very deep. Later, when anyone was proposed as a live-in husband, Yu also discussed it with Cai, and Cai always found a way to break it off. Meanwhile he first bribed You Shi’s natal family.

paragraphs.zh: 布谋已定，自言于玉曰：“吾与令郎至知，本无自赘之理。但事有经权，试与尊叔自筹之。”玉曰：“尊见何如？”彩曰：“吾欲以叔产业悉付我理，请叔族亲议立文书，递年几多供应尊叔夫妇食用，几多供应祭坟纳役，餘者悉付叔存之，以备二孙婚娶；令媳与我为次室。况我拙荆颇贤，必无妒恚之患。后倘得产男女，必不亏她。是令媳得所归，而公家亦有所付托矣。”媳曰：“古云‘宁作贫人妻，莫作富人妾。’我夫与他为友，我嫁他为妾，似不好观瞻。请公公再详。”玉曰：“难得此人家富忠厚，况又代我理家。我不劳而坐享衣食，餘剩者又存与孙婚娶。文字有我族人为证，何等安妥，不必再疑。”海军家大小皆以为然，游氏父母亦同声曰“可”，游氏只得听命。
paragraphs.en: When the plot was set, he said to Yu himself, “I was on the closest terms with your son; there is no reason I should move in. But affairs have the constant and the expedient. Try thinking it through with your own mind.” Yu said, “What is your view?” Cai said, “I would have your property all put in my charge. Please have your clan kin draw up a document: so much each year to supply you and your wife with food and use, so much for ancestral graves and labor service; the rest to be kept for you, to provide for the two grandsons’ marriages. Let your daughter-in-law be my second wife. My own humble wife is quite worthy; there will surely be no jealousy. Later, if there are sons or daughters, I will not short her. So your daughter-in-law will have a place, and the public household will have someone to trust.” The daughter-in-law said, “The old saying is, ‘Better a poor man’s wife than a rich man’s concubine.’ My husband was his friend; if I marry him as a concubine, it will not look well. Please, Father-in-law, consider again.” Yu said, “It is hard to find a house so rich and honest, and he will manage for us besides. I sit and enjoy clothes and food without labor; the remainder is saved for the grandsons’ marriages. The writing is witnessed by my clansmen. How secure that is; no need to doubt further.” The Pan household, old and young, all thought it right; You Shi’s parents also said together, “Agreed.” You Shi had no choice but to obey.

paragraphs.zh: 不觉嫁后二十餘载，生有二子，又养一长孙。前二子皆已娶媳，亦生二孙。彩之正室前十年已故，游氏与夫极和顺。一日，大雨如注，天井水满。忽有青蛙浸于水中，跃起庭上。彩以小竹挑入水中去，如此者数次。彩平时是谨密之人，是日天牖其衷，暗忖游氏恩情已久，谅谈前情，妻必不怨，不觉漏言曰：“你前夫亦似此青蛙。若不生计较，安得与你成夫妇？”游氏曰：“计较若何？”彩曰：“昔时见你貌无双，要得同床伴我眠。心生一计同贸易，过渡踢他落波心。你夫奔起浮水面，再将篙指落深渊。连奔连指两三次，亦如青蛙此状情。”游氏惊号，大骂曰：“你这狼子野心贼，当千刀万剐！哪有人如此狠心者！”彩被妻骂，无一语可应之。游氏哭奔于路，高声叫曰：“我前夫被这贼谋死，谋我为妾！我必经官告论，为前夫报仇！”左邻右舍皆卒听惊骇。彩叫二子强抬游氏入家，皆跪下苦劝曰：“看家中大小之面，勿说此话。”游氏指骂二子曰：“你父奸谋子岂昌，无端造恶忒强梁。险邪暗害同曹贼，天牖其衷自说扬。呈官告论清奸孽，斩他首级振纲常。我夫虽然归黄土，九泉之下也心凉。”
paragraphs.en: Unawares, more than twenty years after the marriage, she had borne two sons and raised an eldest grandson. The two earlier sons had both taken wives and also had two grandsons. Cai’s principal wife had died ten years before; You Shi and her husband were extremely harmonious. One day rain poured down; the courtyard well filled with water. Suddenly a frog, soaked in the water, leaped onto the hall. Cai used a small bamboo to poke it back into the water, several times like this. Cai was ordinarily a close-mouthed man, but that day Heaven opened his breast. He thought You Shi’s affection had lasted long; if he spoke of the past she would surely not resent it, and without noticing he let it slip: “Your former husband was like this frog.
